subtopic: Preparing for a science or robotics competition
subtype: Approach: testing repeatedly and logging failures [Action]
passage: I'm Lalit. Hrithik and I ran our robot fifty times on the mock track and wrote every failure in a log: run number, what went wrong, our guess at why. Twenty-two of the fifty were the same thing, the left wheel wobbling loose. Eleven were sensor glare from the window. The rest looked random, and nobody wanted to chase the random ones. So we tightened the wheel, checked every screw before each run, and taped a card over the sensor as a shade. Then we ran fifty more. Forty-one finished. Looking back, the log changed how I felt about failing: from it keeps going wrong to here is the list, and we can fix number one first.

qa.q: How many of the fifty runs failed because of the loose left wheel?
qa.a: Twenty-two of the fifty were the wobbling left wheel.

qa.q: How did the log change what Lalit felt about the failures?
qa.a: Lalit went from feeling stuck to feeling hopeful, since a written list made the problems fixable one at a time.

qa.q: What else could the team try?
qa.a: They could test at different times of day or in another room to check the glare problem, and keep logging the results.

qa.q: How might Hrithik see the log?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel relieved to have evidence instead of arguments, since Hrithik helped run the tests and record them.

grounding: Students run the robot fifty times on a mock track, log each failure and cause, and fix the most frequent problem first, such as a loose wheel or sensor glare.
